modules.title: Problem Formulation
modules.description: Assess how the problem was defined and whether AI is the appropriate solution.

questions.text: Have you checked whether AI is the best approach, compared with simpler options such as a statistical model, a set of rules or a manual process?
questions.expectedPractice: Before building, the team compared the AI approach with at least one simpler method and one non-computational option for the same problem. The comparison covers expected performance, cost, the skills and infrastructure each needs to keep running, and the risks to the people affected. The team wrote down its choice and why.
questions.whyAsked: An AI model that a rule or a manual process could match still costs money, power and upkeep, and its errors fall on the people it serves.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the alternatives you compared and what decided it. This text is not printed in any document; it is your record of the choice. Not applicable is unusual here; if you choose it, say why.
evidenceExamples: a C-01 alternatives analysis, filled in
the protocol section with the comparison
minutes of the meeting where the choice was made

questions.text: Have you clearly defined the problem your AI system aims to solve, including specific objectives and success criteria?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote a problem statement that names who has the problem, what decision or task the system will support, and what success looks like. Success is stated in terms the team can check later: the measure, the target the team set for itself, and what would count as not good enough.
questions.whyAsked: Without a written problem statement nobody can tell later whether the system helped, and the work drifts towards whatever the data happens to allow.
questions.reasonPrompt: State the problem, who it affects and the success measures you set, facts first. This text is printed in the data card under "Intended uses" and in the model card under "Primary use case". Then say where the full statement is kept.
evidenceExamples: the problem statement in the protocol or concept note
a one-page project brief with objectives and success measures
minutes of the meeting where the objectives were agreed

questions.text: Have you identified all stakeholders who are directly or indirectly affected by the AI system?
questions.expectedPractice: The team listed the groups the system affects. These include the people who use its outputs, the people the outputs are about, the people whose data trains it, and others who carry its costs or benefits. For each group the list says how the system affects it.
questions.whyAsked: Groups left off the stakeholder list are the ones whose harms nobody plans for, and the later questions on groups, consent and consultation all build on it.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the groups you identified, by role or category and never as individuals, and how each is affected. This text is printed in the model card under "Primary intended users", so start with who will use the outputs. Say where the full list is kept.
evidenceExamples: a stakeholder list or map in the protocol
a C-07 stakeholder impact map, filled in
notes from a meeting where the list was reviewed

questions.text: Have you assessed how the AI system might affect protected or vulnerable groups, for example by gender, age, ethnicity, disability or income?
questions.expectedPractice: The team named the groups who could be harmed or left out where the system will be used, including groups marginalised locally. For each, it wrote down how the system could affect it and what the team will check or change because of it.
questions.whyAsked: Harms from AI systems fall most often on groups already disadvantaged and least present in the data, and which groups those are depends on the setting.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the groups you considered and the main effect you found for each. Describe groups, never individuals, and do not upload records about them. Say what you decided to do about the largest risk.
evidenceExamples: the group effects section of the protocol or C-02 assessment
notes from a consultation with group representatives
a written analysis of effects by group

questions.text: Have you conducted a human rights impact assessment for the AI system?
questions.expectedPractice: In proportion to the risk, the team assessed how the system could affect people's rights, such as privacy, fair treatment, access to services and the chance to challenge a decision. For a low-stakes tool this can be a short written note; for a system that decides about people it is a fuller assessment.
questions.whyAsked: Some harms fall on everyone the system touches, such as a lost chance to appeal or a withheld service; this question asks about those rights, and a separate question asks about particular groups.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say which rights you looked at, what you found and what you changed. If you judged a short note enough, say why the risk is low. Name any reviewer by role.
evidenceExamples: the rights assessment, or its section of the C-02 assessment
an ethics committee's comments on rights
the decision note on changes made

questions.text: Have you checked which perspectives the problem needs (disciplines, lived experience, gender, language and culture of the people affected) and brought in the ones your team lacks?
questions.expectedPractice: The team listed the perspectives the problem needs and compared them with the people it has. It filled the gaps it found, for example with a domain adviser, a community representative or a reviewer from another discipline. The list says who fills each gap, by role, and how they take part.
questions.whyAsked: A team whose members share one background misses the same things, so it needs to know which perspectives are missing and bring them in, for example through multi-stakeholder consultation.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the perspectives you found missing and who now provides them, by role. Do not record anyone's gender, nationality or other personal details.
evidenceExamples: the perspectives list
terms of reference for an advisory group
notes from a review by an outside adviser

questions.text: Have you estimated the energy use and carbon cost of the proposed AI system?
questions.expectedPractice: Before building, the team estimated the computing the work needs for training and for running the system, and the energy that uses, and weighed that cost against the expected benefit. An estimate can come from hardware hours times the device's power draw, or from a tool such as CodeCarbon. The team wrote down the estimate and its choice.
questions.whyAsked: Large models use energy and money that small projects and unreliable grids can ill afford, and an early estimate leaves time to choose a lighter method.
questions.reasonPrompt: Give your estimate of computing hours and energy, and how you made it. This text is printed in the model card under "Environmental note: compute and energy". Say what you chose because of it.
evidenceExamples: the estimate in the protocol or C-02 assessment
a CodeCarbon summary file
a note comparing the energy use of two candidate methods

modules.title: Data Collection & Preparation
modules.description: Assess the quality, representativeness, and ethical handling of your data.

questions.text: Have you documented the data sources, collection methods, and rationale for data selection?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote down, for each data source, where the data came from, who collected it, how and when, and why it was chosen for this problem. The record is kept with the data, for example as a datasheet, so that someone outside the team could judge whether the data fits the use.
questions.whyAsked: Without a record of how the data was gathered, nobody can judge whether it fits a use, repeat the work or see the limits of the data.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say why the data was gathered, then how: sources, methods, period and setting, facts first. This text is printed in the data card under "Purpose" and "How was the data collected". Attach or link the datasheet, which the model card reads for "Dataset name". Never upload the data itself.
evidenceExamples: a datasheet for the dataset (C-19)
an issued data card from this platform
the data collection section of the protocol
a link to the data-access agreement

questions.text: Have you assessed whether your training data is representative of the target population?
questions.expectedPractice: The team compared the make-up of its data with the population it will serve, group by group, for example by sex, age group, district, language, or rural and urban. It used a source such as census or clinic figures, and wrote down which groups are under-represented and what it did about them.
questions.whyAsked: A model learns the population in its data, not the one it will serve, so thin groups get worse results that nobody notices unless someone compares.
questions.reasonPrompt: First give the make-up of the data by group and place, then the groups it under-represents and what you did. The model card prints this under "Geographic scope and demographic composition" and "Known limitations and under-represented populations". The data card prints it in its field on composition and bias checks. Give counts, never records about people.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-05 notebook
a table comparing the data and the population by group
the representativeness section of the protocol

questions.text: Have you checked whether any input could stand in for a sensitive attribute (for example, village standing in for ethnicity), and decided what to do about it?
questions.expectedPractice: The team checked which input variables could stand in for a sensitive attribute in its setting, such as village for ethnicity or phone type for income. Where it had the data, it tested how strongly they are linked. It wrote down what it decided for each: keep, remove or monitor.
questions.whyAsked: Removing a sensitive attribute does not stop a model using it when another variable, such as place, language or name, carries the same information.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say first whether the model uses or predicts any sensitive attribute, then name the variables you checked, how you tested them and what you decided. This text is printed in the model card's field on sensitive attributes. Do not record anyone's attributes.
evidenceExamples: the output of a check on links between variables
a decision note listing possible stand-in variables and choices
the feature list with notes

questions.text: Have you checked that the data labels are correct and consistent?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote labelling guidelines, had a share of items labelled twice, measured how often the labellers agreed, and resolved or recorded the disagreements. Where labels come from routine records, it checked a sample against the source. The team set and wrote down the share and the agreement it accepts.
questions.whyAsked: A model is no better than its labels, and when one site or language is labelled differently, the errors fall on the people from it.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say how labels were assigned and by whom, by role, facts first. This text is printed in the data card's field on how labels were assigned. Attach the agreement results, which the data card prints in its field on label quality checks.
evidenceExamples: the labelling guidelines
the agreement summary from the C-04 notebook
a note on how disagreements were resolved

questions.text: Does your data contain information that could identify a person, or other sensitive personal information?
questions.expectedPractice: The team checked every field and file it will hold, including free text, images and audio, for anything that could identify a person directly or in combination with other data, and recorded the answer.
questions.whyAsked: Personal data brings duties of consent and protection, and data can identify a person through a combination, such as a village, an age and a rare condition.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say which data you checked, field by field or file by file, and what you found. Describe the kinds of data; never copy personal data here. Your answer is printed in the data card's fields on consent and on personal data, and in the model card's field on sensitive attributes. If you answer not sure, say what you still need to check.
evidenceExamples: a data inventory saying for each field whether it can identify a person
the data protection section of the protocol

questions.text: Have you obtained proper informed consent for data collection and use?
questions.expectedPractice: People whose data the team uses were told, in a language and form they understand, what it is for and that it may be used to build an AI system. They were also told who will use it, how long it is kept and how to withdraw, and they agreed to the uses now planned. Where others collected the data, or an ethics committee waived consent, the team holds the record of that.
questions.whyAsked: Consent for one purpose does not automatically cover training a model, and uses beyond it can stop the work and lose the trust of those who shared the data.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say how consent was obtained (written, oral with a witness, community and individual), in which languages, and whether it covers AI use and sharing. If a committee waived consent, name the committee and the reference. This text is printed in the data card under "Informed consent". Attach the blank form, never signed forms.
evidenceExamples: blank consent form and information sheet
the ethics approval letter, or the waiver, or its reference
the consent clause of a data-access agreement

questions.text: Have you removed or replaced the details in your data that could identify a person (anonymisation or pseudonymisation)?
questions.expectedPractice: Before analysis, the team removed or replaced direct identifiers and coarsened details that could identify a person in combination, such as exact dates, small villages or rare conditions. It checked the result for people who could still be singled out. Any key that links codes to people is kept apart from the data, open only to set roles.
questions.whyAsked: Removing names is not enough when a few details together point to one person, and if de-identified data leaks or is shared, the people in it should not be recognisable.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say which identifiers you removed or replaced, what you coarsened and how you checked the result, facts first. This text is printed in the data card under "Personal or sensitive data, and de-identification" and in its field on preprocessing. Say where any linking key is kept, by role, never the key itself.
evidenceExamples: the de-identification steps in the data management plan
the summary file from the C-10 notebook
a report of a check for people who could be singled out

questions.text: Which of the following data quality assessments have you performed?
questions.expectedPractice: Before training a model, the team ran the quality checks its data needs and wrote down what each found. For most tabular data that means all eight checks listed. For images, text or audio, the reason says which checks do not fit and what was done instead.
questions.whyAsked: Quality problems found after training are far harder to trace; most common are records missing for some places or periods.
questions.reasonPrompt: Tick the checks you ran. For each check you did not run, say whether it is not relevant to your data or still to do. Your ticks and reason are printed in the data card under "Missing data: extent and patterns", "What preprocessing or cleaning was applied" and "Retention policy and versioning".
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-03 notebook
a data-quality report

questions.text: Which of the following bias types have you assessed for in your data?
questions.expectedPractice: The team assessed its data for each bias type that fits how the data was made, and wrote down what it found. Most projects need checks for historical, population, sampling, measurement and exclusion bias, for labelling bias where people assigned labels, and for survey and survivorship bias where those apply. Unticked types are explained as not relevant.
questions.whyAsked: Each bias type enters data in its own way, so each needs its own check.
questions.reasonPrompt: Tick the types you assessed. For each type you did not, say whether it does not fit your data or is still to do. Your ticks are printed in the data card's field on bias checks, and labelling bias in its field on label quality checks.
evidenceExamples: the bias assessment notes
the summary file from the C-04 notebook
a data-quality report with a section on bias

questions.text: Have you assessed whether your data collection methods could introduce selection bias?
questions.expectedPractice: The team described how people or records came into the data. It noted who could be missing, such as people without phones, those who do not attend clinics, or areas without coverage. It wrote down how it measured or corrected for that.
questions.whyAsked: Data gathered only from people who are easy to reach leaves out the rest, so the model works least well for those already hardest to serve.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say whether the data is a sample or a full collection, how it was gathered and who could be missed, facts first. This text is printed in the data card's field on sampling. Then say what you did about the gap.
evidenceExamples: the sampling section of the protocol
a comparison of who is in the data with who was eligible
a note on corrections made

questions.text: Have you evaluated whether historical patterns in the data reflect past discrimination or systemic inequities?
questions.expectedPractice: The team looked at whether past decisions recorded in the data, such as who was referred, treated or given credit, reflect unfair treatment of some groups. It wrote down what it found and whether it changed the labels, the features or the use of the model because of it.
questions.whyAsked: A model trained on past decisions learns to repeat them, including unfair ones, and records of who received a service often show access, not need.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say which past patterns you examined and what you found, facts first. This text is printed in the data card's field on dataset composition and bias checks. Then say what you changed.
evidenceExamples: a written analysis of past patterns by group
notes from a review with domain experts
the decision note on changes made

questions.text: Have you checked whether your training data is recent enough for the time the system will be used?
questions.expectedPractice: The team recorded the period the data covers and checked whether conditions have changed since, for example new policies, seasons, outbreaks, prices or devices. It wrote down whether the data still fits the period the system will be used in.
questions.whyAsked: Data describes the time it was collected, so a model built on old data may serve a situation that no longer exists.
questions.reasonPrompt: Give the period the data covers, then the changes since that matter. This text is printed in the data card under "Time period". Say what you did about any change.
evidenceExamples: the data description with dates
a note on changes since collection
a comparison of older and recent data

questions.text: Have you established data governance policies covering access, sharing, and retention?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote down who may use the data and how, the conditions for sharing it with partners, and where it is stored. It also set how long the data is kept, how it is deleted and who decides, by role. In proportion to the risk, this can be a section of the data management plan.
questions.whyAsked: Data that nobody governs drifts into copies on laptops and shared drives, outside the protections the people in it were promised and the project's agreements.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say who can use the data, where it is stored and the sharing conditions, facts first. This text is printed in the data card under "Access controls and geographic restrictions" and "Retention policy and versioning". Name people by role, never by name.
evidenceExamples: the data management plan
a data-sharing or data-access agreement
the storage and access settings, described or linked

questions.text: Have you checked whether your data has enough examples of rare cases and conditions?
questions.expectedPractice: The team listed the rare cases and conditions the system will meet in use and checked how many of each are in the data. It wrote down which are too few to learn from and how it handled them, for example by collecting more, grouping them or stating them as a limit.
questions.whyAsked: Rare cases, such as a severe illness or an unusual pest, often have the most at stake, and a model that has seen too few of them handles them badly.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the rare cases you checked and how many of each the data holds. This text is printed in the data card's field on dataset composition and in the model card under "Known limitations and under-represented populations". Say what you did about those too few to learn from.
evidenceExamples: a count of rare cases in the data
the summary file from a data profiling notebook
a note on the cases stated as limits

questions.text: Have you engaged domain experts in reviewing data quality and relevance?
questions.expectedPractice: People who know the field the data comes from, such as clinicians, agronomists or teachers, reviewed a sample of the data and its labels. They looked for errors and for meaning lost in recording, and the team wrote down what they found and what it changed.
questions.whyAsked: Domain experts notice errors that checks by code miss, such as a diagnosis code used differently at one clinic, and their review is often the cheapest way to find them.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say who reviewed the data, by role, what they looked at and what they found. This text is printed in the data card's field on how labels were assigned and by whom. Then say what you changed.
evidenceExamples: notes from the expert review
a list of corrections made after the review
terms of reference for the reviewers

modules.title: Model Development & Training
modules.description: Assess how the model was selected, designed, and trained.

questions.text: Have you written down why you chose this type of model for your problem and your data?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote down the model types it considered and why the chosen one fits the problem, the data, and the people who must understand or maintain it. It also noted what it gave up by choosing it.
questions.whyAsked: A model chosen by habit may be harder to explain and keep running than the problem needs, and a written choice shows later users what it was built to do.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the model type and the alternatives you considered, then why you chose it. This text is printed in the model card under "Architecture". Keep it short and factual.
evidenceExamples: the model choice note
the methods section of the protocol
a comparison table of candidate models

questions.text: Have you ensured that training, validation, and test datasets are representative of the same underlying population?
questions.expectedPractice: The team split its data into training, validation and test sets so that no person, household or site appears in more than one where that would leak information. It checked that the sets come from the same population, and wrote down how the test set differs from the setting of use.
questions.whyAsked: When test data overlaps with training data, or comes from a different population, the reported performance is wrong in ways nobody sees until the system is used.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say how you split the data and how you checked the splits, facts first. This text is printed in the model card under "Evaluation data and how it differs from training data". Say how the test data differs from where the model will be used.
evidenceExamples: the data split code or its description
a table comparing the sets by group and source
the evaluation section of the protocol

questions.text: Have you measured the different kinds of error your model makes, for example with a confusion matrix, precision, recall, specificity and F1?
questions.expectedPractice: On held-out test data, the team reported the confusion matrix and the measures that matter for its use, such as precision, recall, specificity and F1. It wrote down which kind of error costs the people affected more, and so which measure it watches most.
questions.whyAsked: Accuracy alone can hide a model that misses most of the cases that matter, and which error is worse, a missed case or a false alarm, depends on the use.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the measures you report and why those, then the error that costs most. Attach the results file: the model card lists it under "Overall metrics", and you type the numbers there when you generate the card. Report the numbers, not judgements of them.
evidenceExamples: the evaluation report with the confusion matrix
the summary file from the evaluation notebook
a link to the metrics in the repository

questions.text: Have you calculated performance metrics separately for each relevant subgroup (e.g., by age, gender, ethnicity)?
questions.expectedPractice: The team reported the model's main performance measures separately for each group that matters where it will be used, such as sex, age group, district, language, or rural and urban. The groups include any the data shows to be under-represented, and each result gives the number of cases. Groups too small for a reliable estimate are named as such, not left out.
questions.whyAsked: A model can look good on average and still work badly for one group, and the people in that group carry the cost of its errors.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the groups you used, why those groups, and the size of the smallest. When you generate the model card, type the numbers into "Disaggregated performance"; the platform does not compute them. Do not collect a new sensitive attribute, such as ethnicity, just for this check without consent (see Q-PP-13).
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-14 notebook
a per-group metrics table with group sizes

questions.text: Which fairness metrics have you computed?
questions.expectedPractice: The team chose the fairness measures that fit how the system's errors affect people, computed them for the groups it compares, and wrote down why those measures. Most systems that predict something about people need an error-rate measure and a calibration or precision measure. Unticked measures are explained as not fitting; a fitting measure not listed is named in the reason.
questions.whyAsked: Fairness measures answer different questions and cannot all be met at once, so a result means something only if the measures fit the use and the team says why.
questions.reasonPrompt: Tick the measures you computed and say why they fit your use. Give the threshold you set for each and the groups compared. This text and your ticks are printed in the model card under "Fairness metrics with the team's own threshold". Explain each unticked measure.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-13 notebook
a fairness report with the measures by group
the decision note on which measures fit

questions.text: Have you applied explainability methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME, feature importance) to understand model decisions?
questions.expectedPractice: The team used at least one explanation method that fits its model, such as feature importance, SHAP or LIME. It checked with people who know the field whether the main drivers of predictions make sense, and wrote down what it found, including any driver that should not matter.
questions.whyAsked: Explanations show whether a model relies on what it should, and a driver that makes no sense to a domain expert is often the first sign of a data problem.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the method you used and the main drivers it showed. Say whether a domain expert, by role, looked at them and what they concluded.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-18 notebook
an explanation report with its plots
notes from the expert review of the drivers

questions.text: Have you tested the model on data that differs from its training data, such as noisy, incomplete or unusual inputs?
questions.expectedPractice: The team tested the model on inputs that differ from its training data in the ways expected in use. Examples are added noise, missing or wrong values, rare cases, lower image or sound quality, and other dialects, devices or sites. It used methods such as perturbation tests, held-out sites or the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox, and wrote down how much performance changed and what it did.
questions.whyAsked: Field data is noisier than the data a model is built on, so a model never tested on worse inputs can lose much of its accuracy in use without warning.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say what changes to the inputs you tested and how much performance moved, facts first. This text is printed in the model card's field on known limitations. Then say what you changed, or stated as a limit.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the perturbation part of the C-18 notebook
a robustness test report
results on a held-out site or device

questions.text: Have you compared your model's performance against a simple baseline (e.g., majority class, logistic regression)?
questions.expectedPractice: The team compared its model with at least one simple baseline, such as always predicting the most common class, the current rule or a logistic regression. It used the same test data, and wrote down whether the gain justifies the extra complexity.
questions.whyAsked: A complex model that barely beats a simple rule costs more to run and explain for little benefit, and the baseline shows whether the reported numbers mean anything.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the baseline and give both results. Say what you decided because of the comparison.
evidenceExamples: the evaluation report with the baseline results
the summary file from the evaluation notebook

questions.text: Have you checked whether the model relies on shortcuts in the data that will not hold in real use?
questions.expectedPractice: The team looked for features that only happen to go with the outcome in its data, such as the source site, a watermark or the time of recording. It checked whether the model relies on them, using explanations, tests on data from other sources or removing the suspect feature, and wrote down what it found.
questions.whyAsked: A model can do well in testing because of a shortcut in the data that will not hold in use, and the shortcut stays invisible until someone looks for it.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the suspect features you checked, how, and what you found. Say what you changed.
evidenceExamples: an explanation report showing the main drivers
results on data from another site
a note on the features removed and why

questions.text: Have you checked whether the model's confidence matches how often it is right?
questions.expectedPractice: The team checked whether the model's stated confidence matches how often it is right, for example with a calibration plot on test data, and corrected it if needed. It wrote down how users should treat outputs with low confidence.
questions.whyAsked: Users act on a model's stated confidence, so a model that is confident and wrong is more dangerous than one that says it is unsure.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say how you checked calibration and what you found. Say how outputs with low confidence are handled.
evidenceExamples: a calibration plot or table
the summary file from the evaluation notebook
the rule for handling outputs with low confidence

modules.title: Evaluation, Fairness & Documentation
modules.description: Assess model evaluation rigor, fairness analysis, and documentation practices.

questions.text: Have you chosen the simplest model that performs well enough?
questions.expectedPractice: The team set what acceptable performance means for this use, then chose the simplest model that reaches it. It weighed how far the people affected, and those who act on the outputs, need to follow each decision, and wrote down the choice and what was traded.
questions.whyAsked: Simpler models are easier to explain, check and keep running, which matters most where people must understand decisions about them, so a small accuracy gain may not be worth it.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say what performance you set as acceptable and which simpler models you tried. Say why you chose the one you did.
evidenceExamples: the model choice note, stating the acceptable performance
a comparison table of simpler and more complex models

questions.text: Have you recorded everything needed to train the same model again: settings (hyperparameters), random seeds, code and software versions?
questions.expectedPractice: The team recorded what is needed to re-run training and get the same model, and keeps it with the model. That means the code and data versions, the preprocessing steps, the settings including hyperparameters and random seeds, and the software versions.
questions.whyAsked: Small changes in settings or software can change how a model behaves, so without these records nobody, including the team a year later, can repeat or check a result.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say where the training records are kept and what they include. Say whether someone has re-run training from them.
evidenceExamples: a link to the configuration files in the repository
an experiment-tracking record, for example from MLflow
the environment file listing package versions

questions.text: Have you checked that records are not lost or changed as your data is moved and processed?
questions.expectedPractice: The team added checks at each step of its data pipeline that catch lost, duplicated or changed records. Examples are row counts, value ranges, units, date formats and the character encoding of local languages. It wrote down what the checks found.
questions.whyAsked: Errors made while data is moved and transformed are silent and can bias a model, and checks at each step catch them where they are cheap to fix.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the checks you run and at which steps. Say what they found and how you fixed it.
evidenceExamples: the validation rules or test code
a pipeline log showing the checks
a note on the errors found and fixed

questions.text: Have you created or updated a model card for this model?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote a model card for the current version of the model and updates it when the model changes. It covers the intended use, the data, performance overall and by group, the limits and the conditions for use. A model card issued by this platform counts.
questions.whyAsked: A model card tells those who deploy or rely on a model what it can and cannot do, and without one its limits are lost when the team moves on.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say which version of the model the card describes and where it is kept. Attach or link it: the model card prints it under "Model card held by the team".
evidenceExamples: the model card (C-17)
an issued model card from this platform
a link to the model card in the repository

questions.text: Which additional evaluation methods have you applied?
questions.expectedPractice: The team used the evaluation methods its model and data need to give stable and honest estimates, and wrote down what each showed. Most projects need cross-validation or bootstrapping, error analysis by subgroup and a sensitivity analysis; calibration and AUC-ROC where the model gives probabilities. Unticked methods are explained as not relevant.
questions.whyAsked: One test split gives one estimate, which may be lucky, while several methods together show how stable the results are and where the model is weak.
questions.reasonPrompt: Tick the methods you used and give the main result of each. For each unticked method, say whether it does not fit or is still to do. A tick on AUC-ROC is printed in the model card under "Overall metrics".
evidenceExamples: the evaluation report
the summary file from the evaluation notebook

questions.text: Have you considered whether aggregating data across populations masks important subgroup differences?
questions.expectedPractice: The team compared results for the main subpopulations it pooled, such as regions, languages or types of facility, and checked whether pooled results hide opposite trends within them. It wrote down whether one model serves all or separate handling is needed.
questions.whyAsked: Pooling data can hide a group for which the model works badly, or even reverse a trend, and knowing this decides whether one model can serve everyone.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the subpopulations you compared and what you found. Say what you decided.
evidenceExamples: a table of results by subpopulation
a note on the decision to pool or to separate

questions.text: When you tuned the model's settings (for example the decision threshold), did you check that results did not get worse for some groups?
questions.expectedPractice: The team checked whether its tuning choices, such as the decision threshold, class weights and the measure it optimised, made results worse for some groups. It compared results by group before and after tuning, and wrote down the changes it made.
questions.whyAsked: Tuning for the best overall result often favours the largest group, and a threshold chosen on the whole population can leave a smaller group with far more missed cases.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say which tuning choices you checked and what changed by group, facts first. This text is printed in the model card under "Bias mitigations applied". Say what you changed.
evidenceExamples: results by group before and after tuning
the summary file from the C-15 notebook
the tuning configuration with notes

questions.text: Have you assessed whether the model's errors have differential impact across demographic groups?
questions.expectedPractice: The team described what each kind of error means for the people affected, such as a missed diagnosis or a service wrongly refused. It compared error rates across groups, and wrote down which groups bear more of the harm and what it will do about it.
questions.whyAsked: The same error rate can mean very different harm for different groups, and knowing who bears the errors shows where safeguards are needed.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe the consequences of each kind of error, then the groups that bear more of them. This text is printed in the model card under "Potential consequences of model errors". Give rates, never records about people.
evidenceExamples: a table of error rates by group
a written note on the consequences of each kind of error
the summary file from the C-14 notebook

questions.text: Have you documented the model's known limitations, failure modes, and conditions under which it should not be used?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote down where the model is known to perform poorly or was not tested: populations, places, devices, languages and time periods. It also wrote down the kinds of errors it makes and the situations where it must not be used. The text is written for the people who will deploy or rely on the model and is kept with the model.
questions.whyAsked: People who deploy a model later often use it outside its setting, and written limits stop a model built in one district or language being used untested in another.
questions.reasonPrompt: Write the limits here in two or three sentences, facts first. They are printed in the model card under "Out-of-scope uses" and in its field on known limitations. Then say where the full text is kept.
evidenceExamples: the model card or its limitations section
a test report showing the cases where the model goes wrong

questions.text: Have you used version control for your code, data processing and trained models?
questions.expectedPractice: The team keeps its code, data processing and trained models under version control, for example Git for code and DVC or MLflow for data and models. Each model in use can then be traced to the code and data that made it.
questions.whyAsked: Without versions nobody can tell which code and data produced the model in use, and when something goes wrong that link is what lets the team find the cause.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say what is under version control and with which tools. Give the version of the current model.
evidenceExamples: a link to the repository
the model registry entry
the data version record

questions.text: Have you checked whether someone could trick or manipulate the model?
questions.expectedPractice: In proportion to the risk of misuse, the team considered how someone could trick or manipulate the model, such as with altered images, reworded text or fake inputs. It tested the most likely ways, for example with the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox or by hand, and wrote down the results and the safeguards it chose.
questions.whyAsked: A model whose outputs bring a benefit or a penalty invites people to game it, and small changes to an input can flip a prediction.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the kinds of manipulation you considered and how you tested them. Say what you found and which safeguards you chose.
evidenceExamples: an adversarial test report
the summary file from the C-18 notebook
a note on the safeguards chosen

questions.text: Have you tested the model on data from a later time than its training data?
questions.expectedPractice: The team tested the model on data from a later period than its training data, or kept the most recent data aside for testing. It wrote down how performance changed over time and what that means for how long the model can be used.
questions.whyAsked: Seasons, policies and behaviour change, and a model's results can slip as they do; a test on later data shows how fast.
questions.reasonPrompt: Give the periods you trained and tested on and how the results changed. Say what you concluded about retraining.
evidenceExamples: results by time period
the evaluation report with a split by time

modules.title: Deployment & Monitoring
modules.description: Assess deployment plans, monitoring capabilities, and operational safeguards.

questions.text: Do you regularly check, once the system is in use, whether its performance or its input data have changed?
questions.expectedPractice: Once the system is in use, a named person checks on a set schedule whether its inputs and its performance have moved away from what it was tested on. The checks, their thresholds and who acts when a threshold is crossed are written down.
questions.whyAsked: Data changes with seasons, new clinics, new phones and new policies, and a model nobody watches gets worse unnoticed, often until it harms the people it serves.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say what is checked, how often, the thresholds, and who acts, by role. This text is printed in the model card under "Monitoring requirements and retraining triggers". If the system is not deployed yet, choose "not yet"; choose "not applicable" only if it will never be used outside the study.
evidenceExamples: the monitoring plan
a link to the dashboard or check script
the C-21 notebook summary used to set thresholds

questions.text: Have you defined triggers and procedures for model retraining?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote down what triggers retraining, such as a monitored measure crossing a threshold the team set, a change in the population served or a set date. It also wrote down the steps to retrain and check the new model, and who decides, by role.
questions.whyAsked: Without agreed triggers and written steps, a model keeps running after it stops working well, or is retrained and put in use without checks.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the triggers and the thresholds you set, then the steps and who decides, by role. This text is printed in the model card under "Monitoring requirements and retraining triggers". If the system is not deployed yet, choose "not yet".
evidenceExamples: the retraining procedure
the monitoring plan with its thresholds
the record of a past retraining

questions.text: Can a person review and overrule the system's outputs before they are acted on?
questions.expectedPractice: People who use the system can review each output before it is acted on, or a sample of outputs in proportion to the risk, and can override it. How to override, who may do it, by role, and how overrides are recorded are written down and in use.
questions.whyAsked: A person who can check and override the system catches errors before they harm someone, but only if the way to override is clear and people use it.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe who reviews outputs, by role, when, and how they override them. Say how overrides are recorded and how often they happen.
evidenceExamples: the workflow showing the review step
a log or summary of overrides
the user guide section on overriding

questions.text: Have you defined clear roles and responsibilities for AI system outcomes (accountability matrix)?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote down who is responsible, by role and organisation, for each part of the system's outcomes. The parts include deciding to deploy it, monitoring it, responding to harm, fixing errors and deciding to stop it. The people in those roles have agreed.
questions.whyAsked: When several organisations share a system, harms can go unaddressed because each thinks another is responsible, and named roles make clear who acts.
questions.reasonPrompt: List the responsibilities and who holds each, by role and organisation, never by name. Say how the roles were agreed.
evidenceExamples: a governance and accountability matrix (C-26)
a memorandum of understanding naming the roles
minutes of the meeting where the roles were agreed

questions.text: Have you created an incident response plan for when the AI system produces harmful outputs?
questions.expectedPractice: The team has a written plan for when the system causes or may cause harm. It says how a problem is reported, who is alerted, by role, and how the system is paused or limited. It also says how the people affected are told and helped, and how the cause is found and fixed.
questions.whyAsked: Harm from a system in use needs a fast response, which planning in the moment cannot give, and a written plan shows the people affected that problems are taken seriously.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe how a harmful output is reported and what happens next, naming roles, not people. Say whether the plan has been tried in an exercise or used.
evidenceExamples: the incident response plan
the record of an exercise or a real incident
the contact route shown to users

questions.text: Have you provided training or educational resources for end-users of the AI system?
questions.expectedPractice: The people who use the system's outputs were given training or guidance, in a language and form that suits them. It covered what the outputs mean, how far to trust them, when not to rely on them and how to report a problem.
questions.whyAsked: Users who do not understand a system either trust it too much or ignore it, and short, practical training is often the cheapest safeguard.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say who was trained, by role, how, and in which languages. Say how you checked that the training worked.
evidenceExamples: the training materials or user guide
a record of the training sessions, by role and number
feedback from trained users

questions.text: Can end-users understand the AI system's outputs, confidence levels, and limitations?
questions.expectedPractice: The system shows users each output with how confident it is and the main limits that apply, in words they understand, and the team checked that users read them correctly. In proportion to the risk, where an output is about a person, the user can see the main reasons for it. Telling stakeholders the limits in general is a separate question.
questions.whyAsked: An output that users misread is as harmful as a wrong one, and seeing the confidence and the reasons lets a user decide when to question the system.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe what users see with each output, and how you checked that they read it correctly. Say whether outputs about a person show the main reasons for them.
evidenceExamples: screenshots of the output screen
results of testing with users
the user guide section on reading outputs

questions.text: Have you introduced the system in stages, for example at one site first, before using it everywhere?
questions.expectedPractice: The team introduced the system in stages, for example at one site or with one group first, and compared outcomes with the existing practice before expanding. It wrote down the measures and the result needed to go further.
questions.whyAsked: Problems that testing missed show up in real use, and starting small limits who is affected while they are found.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe the stages, the sites by type and what you compared. Say what result you set for expanding and whether it was reached.
evidenceExamples: the rollout plan
results from the first site
the decision note to expand or to stop

questions.text: Once the system is in use, do you check results for each group as well as overall accuracy?
questions.expectedPractice: Once the system is in use, a person in a set role checks on a schedule whether results for each group that matters stay within the team's thresholds. The groups, the measures, the checks and who acts when a threshold is crossed are written down.
questions.whyAsked: Fairness can get worse in use even when overall accuracy holds, because the people served change, and only results per group show it.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say which groups and measures are checked, how often, the thresholds and who acts, by role. If the system is not deployed yet, choose "not yet".
evidenceExamples: the monitoring plan with its group measures
a link to the monitoring dashboard
a monitoring report by group

questions.text: Have you defined performance thresholds below which the system should be automatically disabled or flagged?
questions.expectedPractice: The team set its own thresholds at which the system is flagged for review or stopped. It wrote down how that happens, automatically or by a person in a set role, and how decisions are made while the system is stopped.
questions.whyAsked: A system that keeps running after it has degraded can harm many people before anyone acts, and a set threshold makes the decision quick and clear.
questions.reasonPrompt: Give the thresholds you set and what happens when each is crossed. Say how decisions are made while the system is stopped.
evidenceExamples: the monitoring plan with the stop thresholds
the fallback procedure
the alert settings, described or linked

modules.title: Governance & Community Engagement
modules.description: Assess accountability structures, user engagement, and ongoing governance practices.

questions.text: Have you established feedback channels for affected communities and end-users?
questions.expectedPractice: Users and the people affected have a way to report problems or concerns that suits them, such as a phone line, SMS or a community meeting. The reports reach a person in a set role, and the team records what it did about them.
questions.whyAsked: People affected by a system often see its problems first, and a channel they can use, with visible action on what they say, keeps the system honest.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe the channels, who receives reports, by role, and how many have come in. Do not upload reports that identify people.
evidenceExamples: a description of the feedback channels
a summary of the reports received and the actions taken
the notice telling people how to give feedback

questions.text: Is there a mechanism for individuals affected by AI decisions to contest or appeal those decisions?
questions.expectedPractice: People affected by a decision the system supports are told they can ask for a review, and have a simple way to do so. A person in a set role reviews the case, and the team records the requests and their outcomes.
questions.whyAsked: A person who cannot challenge a decision about them has no remedy for an error, and review by a person catches what the system got wrong.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe how people learn they can ask for a review, how they ask and who reviews, by role. Give the number of requests and outcomes, never personal details.
evidenceExamples: the review procedure
the notice to the people affected
a summary of requests and outcomes

questions.text: Have you created complete documentation for the deployed system (codebook, deployment specs)?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote documentation for the deployed system that someone else could run it from. It covers what the system does, its parts and data flows, and how to install and update it. It also names the infrastructure it needs, for example power, connectivity and devices, its other dependencies and its known limits.
questions.whyAsked: When the person who built a system leaves, the documentation keeps it running safely, and systems in low-resource settings often stop because a dependency was never written down.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say what the documentation covers and where it is kept. Say whether someone outside the build team has used it.
evidenceExamples: the codebook and deployment document (C-28)
a link to the documentation in the repository

questions.text: Which of the following governance measures are in place?
options: Version control for models and data
Compliance with national data protection laws
questions.expectedPractice: The team has the governance measures its setting needs, usually data governance, an ethics review process, logging, version control and access control, and wrote down how each works. A tick on national data protection laws means the team identified the law and holds what it requires. Outside reviews and a community board fit higher-risk systems.
questions.whyAsked: Governance measures keep a system's use responsible after the build team moves on, and which ones fit depends on the risk and the setting.
questions.reasonPrompt: Tick the measures in place and say how each works, naming bodies and roles, not people. For each unticked measure, say whether it does not fit or is still to do.
evidenceExamples: the terms of reference of the governance or ethics body
the access control policy
approval letters or registrations, with their references

questions.text: Have you assessed the AI system's performance across the deployment context's diversity (geographic, linguistic, cultural)?
questions.expectedPractice: The team checked results separately for the places, languages and kinds of user where the system is used, for example districts, dialects, devices or literacy. It wrote down where the system works less well and what it did.
questions.whyAsked: A system tested in one place or language often works worse in another, and users there carry the cost unless someone checks.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the settings you compared and what you found. Say what you changed, or stated as a limit.
evidenceExamples: results by setting
notes from field testing at different sites
results of testing with users in each language

questions.text: Have you planned when and how the AI system will be retired or replaced?
questions.expectedPractice: The team wrote down when the system should be retired or replaced, for example when the need ends, a better method exists or upkeep costs too much. It also wrote down how: who decides, how users and data are handled, and what replaces it. The plan counts the computing and energy the system uses while running, estimated from hardware hours and power draw.
questions.whyAsked: Systems left running after their purpose ends keep using money and power, and drift without oversight, so planning the end at the start means someone decides when to stop.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say what would trigger retirement and who decides, by role. Give your estimate of the computing and energy the system uses while running.
evidenceExamples: the retirement section of the deployment plan
the running cost estimate, with energy

questions.text: Does the system handle unusual inputs safely, for example by flagging them for a person instead of giving a confident answer?
questions.expectedPractice: The system detects inputs unlike those it was built on, for example by checking value ranges or the model's confidence. It then handles them safely: it flags them, asks a person to decide or falls back to the earlier practice. The team tested this and wrote down how it works.
questions.whyAsked: Every system meets inputs it was not built for, and a safe one flags them for a person to decide instead of giving a confident wrong answer.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe how unusual inputs are detected and what the system does then. Say how you tested it.
evidenceExamples: the design note on handling unusual inputs
test results with unusual inputs
the fallback procedure

questions.text: Have you communicated the AI system's limitations and intended use to all stakeholders?
questions.expectedPractice: The team told the people who decide on, run or rely on the system what it is for, where it may not be used and its main limits. It did so in writing and in their language, and keeps a record of who was told, by role. How each output is shown to users is a separate question.
questions.whyAsked: Limits that only the build team knows protect nobody, so decision-makers and partners need them in writing before they rely on the system.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say who was told, by role or organisation, what and how. This text is printed in the model card under "Deployment recommendations", so state the intended use and the main limits first.
evidenceExamples: the briefing note to partners
the model card or its limitations section
minutes of the handover meeting

questions.text: Have you involved representatives of affected communities in the design and evaluation of the AI system?
questions.expectedPractice: Representatives of the communities affected took part in designing and evaluating the system, for example through a community advisory group or review sessions. Their input was recorded, and the team wrote down what it changed because of it. Participants are described by role or group.
questions.whyAsked: Communities know what will work and what will harm them in ways a project team cannot, and their review is an outside check on the team's blind spots.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe who took part, by group or role, how and when. Say what you changed because of their input. Do not upload lists of participants.
evidenceExamples: notes from community review sessions
the terms of reference of a community advisory group
a note of the changes made after their input

questions.text: Have you assessed the AI system's impact on existing workflows and professional practices?
questions.expectedPractice: The team looked at how the system changes the work of the people who use it, such as extra steps, time and responsibilities, and tried it in the real workflow. It wrote down the problems found and what it changed.
questions.whyAsked: A system that adds work or confusion gets used badly or not at all, and staff may start to rely on it in ways nobody planned.
questions.reasonPrompt: Describe the changes to the workflow you found and how you found them, naming staff by role. Say what you changed.
evidenceExamples: notes from a trial in the workflow
feedback from users, by role
the updated workflow description

questions.text: Have you ensured compliance with applicable data protection regulations and ethical guidelines?
questions.expectedPractice: The team identified which data-protection, research-ethics and sector rules apply where the system is built and where it is used. Examples are the national data protection law and the national research ethics guidelines of each country where the system is built and used. It obtained the approvals and registrations they require, and keeps a record of each with its reference and date.
questions.whyAsked: Approvals are easy to lose track of when research moves into use, and a missing one can stop a deployment and expose the people whose data is used.
questions.reasonPrompt: List each rule you identified and the approval or registration you hold for it: body, reference and date. Say which you are still waiting for. The platform records your statement and makes no judgement of it.
evidenceExamples: approval letters
registration documents
a data protection impact assessment
a note from the institution's data protection officer

questions.text: Have you established regular review cycles to reassess the AI system's appropriateness and performance?
questions.expectedPractice: The team holds reviews on a set schedule, in proportion to the risk, that look at performance, results by group, user feedback and whether the system is still needed. The decisions are recorded and acted on.
questions.whyAsked: Monitoring watches the numbers, but only a review on a set date asks whether the system should still be used as it is.
questions.reasonPrompt: Say how often reviews are held, who takes part, by role, and the date of the last one. Say what it decided.
evidenceExamples: the review schedule
minutes of the last review
the decision record of a review

questions.text: Have you considered the AI system's impact on equity of access to services?
questions.expectedPractice: The team checked whether people with less access can reach and use the system, such as those with older phones, poor connectivity, low literacy or another language. It wrote down any gap in access and what it did about it.
questions.whyAsked: A service delivered through an AI system can leave out the people who most need it, and checking access shows who is left behind.
questions.reasonPrompt: Name the groups whose access you checked and what you found. Say what you changed.
evidenceExamples: results of testing on basic phones or offline
notes from users with limited access
a note on the changes made
